generatedProse.concept-context: Familiarise yourself with your psychology module's outcomes before you do anything else. Make notes on them. Each one uses a verb that signals the kind of performance expected, whether that is to describe a theory, to apply a method, to analyse data or to evaluate the strength of a study. That verb is a strong clue to how the assessment will be marked. Checking your work against the outcomes as you go is a quick way to see whether you are doing what the module actually asks, because psychology assessment is intentionally aligned to those outcomes.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students read the same learning outcome from their module handbook: Evaluate the usefulness of a self-report questionnaire for studying anxiety.

Tom reads it quickly and starts describing the method: what a questionnaire is, how it is administered, where it is used. The writing is accurate, but it only describes. The outcome asked for something the writing never does.

Amara reads the same outcome and breaks it down first. The verb is evaluate, which means weighing strengths against weaknesses to reach a judgement. What it is about is the method's usefulness for anxiety specifically, not simply how it works. Demonstrating it means coming to a reasoned view, backed by evidence, about when a questionnaire helps and when it misleads, for example through social desirability bias. Amara then writes to exactly that.

Both students know the method. Only Amara answered the outcome, because only Amara worked out what it was asking.
generatedProse.summary: Learning outcomes state what each psychology module expects you to be able to do, and they are where your assessment points, by design. You can now find the outcomes in your own module's documentation, and break one down into its active verb and what it asks you to demonstrate. Reading outcomes this way turns a vague aim into a clear target, which matters in a discipline where describing a study and evaluating it earn very different marks.

check.body: You are breaking down a psychology learning outcome that begins with the verb 'analyse'. Which of these shows you have understood what that verb asks for?

items.text: Separating the findings or data into their parts, examining how they relate, and saying what that shows.
Listing everything you can remember about the topic.
Giving your personal opinion of the study.
Describing the study clearly from start to finish.

feedback.correct: That's right. To analyse is to break something into its parts, examine how they relate, and say what that shows, which is more than listing, opinion or description.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what 'analyse' asks for that listing, opinion or description do not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: To analyse is to separate the findings or data into their parts, examine how they relate, and say what that shows. Listing, giving an opinion and describing are each doing something the verb does not ask for.
